Firms: Chapter four. Big firms and small.

Behind the industries are firms, and they come in every size. In 2022 America had 6.4 million private businesses with at least one employee. Most are tiny: four million of them, almost two in three, had fewer than five people on the payroll. Now look at the other side. Those four million tiny firms employed about five percent of all private payroll workers. At the far end were 2,262 firms with five thousand or more employees: about one firm in every three thousand. They employed 36 percent of the workers, and made 46 percent of all the sales. And the 546 largest, with twenty thousand or more each, employed a quarter of everyone working for a private business. Small firms are most of the firms. Big firms are most of the jobs.

How big the firms are depends on the industry. In retail, half of all the jobs are in firms with twenty thousand or more employees: Walmart, Amazon, Target, Kroger, Home Depot. Transport and warehousing, the office services that hire out cleaners and guards, information, finance: all above a third. Near the bottom, construction, with three jobs in a hundred in giant firms, and the repair shops, hair salons and laundries, with two. The pattern has a logic. Where one company can spread the same system, brand and buying power over thousands of stores, routes or branches, the giants win. Where the work is done on site, locally and by hand, small firms do. Part five of this series asks why some industries end up with a few firms and others with thousands, and Part seven how to measure who has what share.
Jobs: Chapter six. The economy by jobs.

Now draw the same economy by jobs. In 2025 American employers had 158 million people on their payrolls. The biggest blocks are government, health care and professional and business services, each with more than 22 million jobs, then restaurants, hotels and entertainment with 17 million, and shops with 15. Manufacturing employs 12.6 million people, about one job in twelve. Compare the two maps. Real estate and finance are a fifth of the value added and six percent of the jobs; restaurants and hotels are four percent of the value added and more than ten percent of the jobs.

Divide one map by the other and you get the value added per job. At the top are industries where a few people run a great deal of equipment or property: utilities, about 845 thousand dollars per job, mining, and information, which includes software and telecoms. Real estate and finance look highest of all, but the homeowners' rent inflates them. At the bottom are industries where the work is done by people, face to face: health care, about 100 thousand dollars per job, private education, and restaurants and hotels, 76 thousand. This is not a measure of how hard anyone works. It is a measure of how much machinery, property and software stands behind each worker, and of the prices the industry can charge. A nurse's hour cannot be made by a machine; an hour of electricity can.

Does the value a job adds show up in its pay? Partly. In 2025 the average hour of work in a private business paid 36 dollars 44. In information and in the utilities, about 52 dollars 59. In shops, about 25 dollars 46, and in restaurants and hotels, 22 dollars 84. But look at the spread. From the lowest-paid industry to the highest, pay rises about 2.3 times. Value added per job, in the previous chart, rose about 11 times. Pay is set in a labour market that all industries share: a cashier could become a clerk at the power company, if hired. So pay varies far less than what a job adds, and the rest of the difference goes somewhere else. The next chapter follows it.
Buyers: There is a second way to measure an economy: not by who makes things, but by who finally buys them. In 2023 American households bought 18.8 trillion dollars of goods and services for themselves, 68 percent of the total. Businesses investing in buildings, machines and software, and families buying new homes, which also count as investment: 4.9 trillion. Governments: 4.7 trillion, most of it the work of their own teachers, soldiers and officials. Buyers abroad: 2.6 trillion of American exports. That adds up to 31 trillion. But 3.4 trillion of what those buyers bought was made abroad, so it comes off. What is left, 27.7 trillion dollars, is America's GDP for 2023: exactly the total that the industries' value added gave, counted from the other end of the table.

Each industry has its own customers. Health care, schools, shops, restaurants and hotels sell almost entirely to households. That includes care paid for by Medicare and Medicaid, which the statisticians count as households' spending, because households receive it. Factories sell half to households, a quarter as machinery and equipment that businesses invest in, and a fifth abroad. Business services sell more than half as investment, because software and research now count as investment. Builders sell almost nothing to households as consumption: houses, offices and factories are investment, roads and schools are the government's. Mines and oil fields sell more than half abroad. And the government is its own biggest customer. This matters when times turn. Households keep buying food, rent and health care through a recession. Investment is the buyer that cuts back first and most, so the industries that sell to it, the builders, the machine makers and the software houses, feel a downturn first and hardest. Part six is about that cycle.
Household: Chapter twelve. A household's dollar, followed back.

Now Part one's device, the Dollar, for the whole economy. Take one dollar that an American household spends, and follow it back through Leontief's table to everyone who earns a piece of it. First, what the dollar buys. 24 cents goes on housing and finance, most of it rent; 21 on health care and education; 17 to the shops and wholesalers for the service of selling; 16 on goods and energy at the factory gate; 9 in restaurants, hotels and places of fun; and two cents on the services that businesses sell, such as advertising, law and software. Now follow every cent back, through every supplier, round after round, to the wages and profits of the people who made it. Health and education keep 13 of their 21 cents; the rest pays for medicines, equipment and the services they buy. Goods and energy keep about 11 of 16. The biggest surprise is business services. Households hardly buy them, two cents, yet 11 cents of the dollar ends up there: the lawyers, accountants, advertisers, software houses, cleaners and temporary staff that every other business hires. And about ten cents leaves the country, as imported goods and the imported parts inside American ones. What you buy and who you pay are not the same thing.

Do the same for the other buyers. Of a household's dollar, about 90 cents stays with American industries. Of a dollar of business investment, only about 84: 16 cents leaves the country, because so much investment is machinery, computers and equipment made abroad, and the largest single share goes to business services, the software and research that count as investment. Of a government's dollar, more than 90 cents stays at home, almost half of it as the pay of the government's own employees. These are the sums behind the arguments about where money should be spent: the same dollar supports very different industries, and very different numbers of jobs, depending on who spends it.
Shift: Chapter thirteen. From factories to services.

Here is the change in people. In 1943, in the middle of the war, almost two American payroll jobs in five were in manufacturing. In 2025, one in twelve. The number of factory jobs peaked in 1979, at 19.4 million; in 2025 it was 12.6 million. Yet the factories did not make less. Their real output, adjusted for prices, was 57 percent higher in 2025 than in 1987. Meanwhile education and health care grew from 1.4 million jobs in 1939 to 27 million.

The prices tell the same story from the other side. Between 2000 and 2025, the pay of an hour of an ordinary worker's time rose 124 percent. The prices of the things that are mostly people's time rose about as fast or faster: school fees and childcare 175 percent, the services of doctors and hospitals 138 percent, a meal in a restaurant 126 percent. The prices of things made in factories barely moved, or fell: a new car 25 percent, clothes about one percent, toys down 74 percent, computers down 92 percent, because the statisticians count each year's faster, bigger machine as more computer for the money. So an hour of work buys far more goods than it did, and about the same amount of care, teaching and cooking. That is why spending, and jobs, flowed towards services, even as factories made more.

Four forces did this. Machines: factories and farms raised output per worker faster than almost any other industry, so the same goods need fewer people. Wants: as people get richer, they spend more of each extra dollar on health, education, travel and advice, and less on more things. Prices: an hour of a nurse, a teacher or a lawyer cannot be sped up like a production line, so services keep getting dearer relative to goods, as the prices just showed. The economist William Baumol called it the cost disease. And trade: from 2000, competition from imports, much of it from China, closed factories that would otherwise have stayed open. Economists still argue about how much each force counts; they agree all four are real.
Growth: Size is one thing; growth is another. Between 2015 and 2025, America's output, adjusted for prices, grew by 27 percent. The fastest-growing industries are almost all about computers. Web search, cloud computing and the other internet services grew 304 percent: about four times as big. The firms that design and run other companies' computer systems, and the software publishers, nearly tripled. Taxis and ride-hailing more than doubled, as the apps turned spare cars into a transport industry. Warehousing grew with online shopping, oil and gas with the shale fields, doctors' offices and clinics with an ageing population. Manufacturing as a whole grew 17 percent, slower than the economy, which is why its share keeps falling even as it makes more. And some industries shrank outright: furniture, paper and the railways by about a sixth, printing by 28 percent, as screens replaced paper. Growth is the Board's ninth row. An industry that grows faster than the economy takes a bigger share of it every year; one that shrinks is managed for cash, consolidated or closed.
Profit: Chapter sixteen. Where the profit is.

Last, the profit. The six American companies with the largest operating profit are all, in one way or another, technology companies: Apple, NVIDIA, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon. Each made between 80 and 133 billion dollars. Walmart, the largest employer, made 30 billion. Divide by the people. NVIDIA made about 3.1 million dollars of operating profit for each of its 42 thousand employees; Walmart about 14 thousand for each of its 2.1 million. That is chapter seven again, at the scale of companies: where the product is software, chips designed once and sold millions of times, or a network everyone has to use, a few people can earn enormous profits. Where the product is a person's work in a shop or a hospital, the value added goes mostly in wages, and the profit per person is small.

Divide each company's profit by its sales and you get its margin: how many cents of each dollar of sales it keeps as operating profit. NVIDIA kept 60 cents. Microsoft 46, Meta 41, Apple and Alphabet 32. Amazon kept 11, more than half of it earned by its cloud. Walmart and UnitedHealth about four cents, and McKesson, the medicine wholesaler, one and a half. A thin margin is not a failure. A wholesaler that keeps a cent and a half of every dollar, but sells its whole stock many times a year, can earn a good return on the money tied up in it. How margin, speed and borrowing combine into that return is the subject of Part three: the accounts.
